title: Fast Feathers, Slow Seeds
markdown:
Zuri loved finding out why things worked. Her best friend was Bloop, a round, shiny robot who was very good at counting. Beep boop. Whirr. Bloop could count puffy clouds or even Zuri’s happy giggles.

One bright sunny day in the park they saw Coach Ellis. Toot toot went his whistle. As they walked, Zuri stopped.

“Look.”

Two bird feeders hung from a big oak. One was stuffed full of seeds, a party for birds. The other had only a tiny sprinkle way down at the bottom. A sparrow sat on the full one and ate as if it had appointments. A robin peered into the thin one, hopped, and tried the full one instead.

“Coach Ellis,” Zuri asked, “why does one feeder have lots of seeds, and the other has only a few?”

Coach Ellis smiled. “What do you think?”

Zuri thought. Bloop whirred. Whirr?

Suddenly — whoosh — Mr. Nutty the squirrel zoomed by. He was the park’s super-speedy feeder-filler. He used two noisy spinning machines.

Flick. Flick. The machine for the full feeder was so fast. Seeds flew out like confetti and filled that feeder in a flash. A seed-blitz. Two pigeons arrived as if they had heard the flick from the other path.

But the other machine went tick… tock… tick… tock. Slow as a sleepy snail. Tick… one seed. Tock… another seed. It took a very long time to get just one little seed to pop out. The nearly empty feeder gained a lonely pip and then waited.

Zuri watched, eyes wide. Bloop’s little light blinked faster and faster. Boop. Boop. Boop. He was counting.

Zuri pointed. “The fast machine went flick, flick, and lots of seeds came out. It filled up all the way.” She looked at the other feeder. “The slow one went tick, tock, and only a little bit came out. It didn’t fill up much at all.”

Coach Ellis nodded. “And what does that tell you about how fast the machines were going and how many seeds ended up in the feeders?”

Zuri’s brain did a happy little flip. “Fast machines put lots in. Slow machines put only a little.”

“That’s right,” said Coach Ellis. “Fast means more seeds. Slow means fewer seeds.”

Bloop beeped. Boop. More seeds. He pointed to the full feeder. Beep. Fewer seeds. He pointed to the nearly empty one.

They stood and watched one more round. Flick, flick, flick — a small hill of seed rose in the first feeder. Tick… tock — a single seed clicked into the second and sat there looking proud of itself. Bloop counted the new seeds aloud, then the old ones, then both together, because that was his idea of a good afternoon.

Coach Ellis chuckled. He did not call it a science secret. “When something happens quickly, you can get more of something. When something happens slowly, you get less.”

Zuri giggled. “So fast makes more, and slow makes less. Not magic. Just the machines.”

Bloop did a happy robot wiggle. Boop. Faster means more. Beep. Slower means less.

Ellis blew the whistle once, softly, so the birds would not take it personally. Zuri did not wonder about bubbles or toy boxes. She helped Nutty tilt the slow machine a little so its tick-tock seed landed in the thin feeder instead of on the path. Bloop logged the count on his tummy screen: lots on the left, little on the right, same park, different speeds.

They sat on the bench while the sparrows finished their appointments. The sun painted the sky pink and orange. Zuri wiped seed dust from Bloop’s shoulder. Nutty packed the machines, the fast one still warm, the slow one still ticking as if it had not heard the news.
